candidateRows: Well-being encompasses both the reduction of suffering and every positive possibility available to conscious beings.
This supplies the secular side's foundational criterion for moral evaluation and connects moral truth to the possible states of conscious beings.
After Peterson identifies avoidance of unnecessary suffering as shared ground, Harris expands the moral objective to include the positive range of conscious experience.
Moral questions have objectively right and wrong answers that humanity can progressively discover by studying what improves or damages life.
The proposition states the central secular moral-realist alternative to both relativism and revealed, arbitrary moral injunctions.
Following discussion of suffering as an accessible starting point, Harris rejects relativism and presents moral inquiry as discovery about human value and flourishing.
Moral conduct is grounded in human universals, while dangerous absolutism is a problem of fundamentalism generally rather than religion alone.
This concedes objective moral differences while resisting the secular case's attempt to identify religious belief as the distinctive source of dogmatic danger.
Harris's claim that moral realism avoids both relativism and faith-based arbitrary injunctions.
Peterson accepts moral realism and human universals but reframes the opposing catastrophe as fundamentalism across religious and secular systems.
Religion is uniquely hospitable to dogmatism because it treats faith without compelling evidence as a virtue rather than an epistemic defect.
This gives the secular side's principal reason for treating religious dogmatism as a special case rather than merely one instance of generic authoritarian certainty.
Peterson's contention that fundamentalism generally, not religious fundamentalism specifically, is the relevant danger.
After Peterson broadens the problem to secular and religious absolutism alike, Harris argues that religion uniquely praises unsupported conviction.
Religious beliefs can be especially dangerous because supernatural rewards and an afterlife can devalue present life and authorize extreme conduct.
The move isolates a mechanism through which religious premises may motivate harms beyond those produced by ordinary political dogmatism.
Peterson's comparison between religious totalitarian systems and equally destructive secular totalitarian systems.
Peterson asks whether belief in God matters when secular regimes have committed comparable atrocities; Harris points to the afterlife as a distinctive variable.
The decisive evil in both religious and secular totalitarianism is evidence-resistant dogmatism, which suppresses correction and must ultimately be enforced by coercion.
This unifies Harris's critique of religion with his account of secular atrocities while preserving opposition to all systems that immunize beliefs from revision.
Peterson's suggestion that Nazi and Soviet dogmas were as pernicious as religious dogmas and require a common explanation.
Harris rejects attributing twentieth-century atrocities to atheism, notes their religion-like structures, and identifies uncorrectable dogma as the overarching problem.
Free discourse must outrank particular dogmas because open speech is the governing process by which dogmatic and totalitarian errors are corrected.
The move advances an institutional answer to dogmatism and establishes open inquiry, rather than any fixed doctrine, as the corrective meta-value.
Harris's argument that dogmatism prevents revision through conversation and therefore relies on coercive enforcement.
Once both speakers identify closed claims of absolute truth as the common danger, Peterson elevates free speech as the mechanism for repairing such errors.
Spiritual experiences may be genuine features of consciousness, but any truth they disclose must transcend culturally contingent religious dogmas.
This preserves spirituality while denying that it validates inherited doctrine, offering a universal psychological framework as a replacement for sectarian religion.
Peterson's insistence that religious buildings, music, art, and practice are significant rather than disposable remnants.
The discussion separates religion from dogmatism; Harris accepts transformative spiritual experience but argues that its truth cannot depend on birthplace or tradition.
Chimpanzee territorial violence shows that group atrocity predates religious doctrine, so its deepest causes lie in evolved tribal aggression rather than surface beliefs alone.
The argument directly challenges religion-centered causal accounts of atrocity by locating the underlying capacity in prehuman coalition and territorial behavior.
Harris's account of religious and secular dogmatism as the principal mechanism producing ideological violence and atrocity.
Peterson recounts chimpanzee raiding behavior and argues that comparable violence without religion makes the human problem deeper than professed doctrine.
Religious texts contain clear harmful injunctions that can rationally lead otherwise ordinary believers toward cruelty and keep modern ethics constrained by ancient doctrine.
This is the secular side's fullest causal case that doctrine adds avoidable suffering beyond tribal instinct and that rehabilitating religion perpetuates obsolete moral frameworks.
Peterson's claim that evolved tribal aggression is deeper than religious belief and independently explains group atrocity.
Harris distinguishes tribal violence from harms generated by sincere doctrinal commitment, using conversion, punishment, slavery, and sexual violence to challenge religious accommodation.
Biblical sentences must be interpreted within the Bible's overarching developmental narrative rather than treated as isolated, self-sufficient moral commands.
This supplies Peterson's principal method for reconciling objectionable passages with the religious tradition and directly shapes the dispute over scriptural authority.
The earlier challenge that religious texts contain plainly unacceptable claims whose wrongness does not depend on interpretive complexity.
After conceding that individual sentences may be wrong, Peterson argues that a complex, developmentally ordered biblical narrative conditions the meaning of its constituent passages.
Reading earlier scripture through later scripture does not make Moses's explicit and brutal laws of war morally acceptable.
The objection tests Peterson's interpretive method against explicit biblical rules and argues that narrative context cannot neutralize their straightforward moral content.
Peterson's claim that the beginning of the Christian Bible must be interpreted in light of its developmental ending.
Harris moves from general interpretive theory to Mosaic warfare laws, maintaining that their instructional form and brutality survive any appeal to the New Testament ending.
Treating scripture as revelation binds believers to a humanly assembled canon containing plainly immoral commands that can be rejected without reading the whole narrative.
This directly supports the secular case against dogmatic scriptural authority by connecting divine authorship claims to continued allegiance to morally indefensible passages.
Peterson's attempt to recover psychological truth from religious texts while contextualizing their objectionable passages within a larger tradition.
Harris accepts that religious literature can contain psychological insights but argues that revelation transforms a selective human anthology into an indivisible authority, preserving cruel commands.
Revelation can be read psychologically as teaching that truthful speech produces redemption when personal and social worlds collapse.
The interpretation exemplifies Peterson's affirmative case that biblical imagery encodes durable psychological truths rather than functioning only as literal prophecy or dogma.
Harris's argument that prophecy and apocalyptic scripture encourage dangerous expectations of a glorious end followed by punishment of unbelievers.
Peterson reframes Revelation's apocalypse as a representation of unavoidable collapse and loss, with the birth of the hero and truthful speech symbolizing possible redemption.
Sophisticated metaphorical theology becomes increasingly unconstrained by scripture and can project preferred psychological insights onto almost any text.
This attacks the reliability of Peterson's interpretive method, arguing that its flexibility prevents biblical stories from providing distinctive or objective moral knowledge.
Peterson's psychological interpretation of Revelation as expressing collapse, heroic renewal, and redemption through truthful speech.
Harris allows that interpretations vary in plausibility but contends that theology retreats from literal readings when they become absurd or barbaric, thereby gaining arbitrary freedom.
Christianity embodies the shared antidote of free truthful expression as the redeeming Word, turning an abstract universal principle into a lived personality.
This is a direct affirmative bridge between an agreed secular value and Christian symbolism, supporting the claim that religious stories embody indispensable practical truths.
Harris's contention that Revelation remains dangerous and exclusionary despite flexible literary or psychological reinterpretation.
Peterson argues that both speakers already accept truthful speech as an antidote to dogmatism and totalitarianism, while Christianity uniquely represents that truth as embodied action.
Facts cannot yield values without an a priori interpretive framework, and that mediating framework is partly best understood as personality or story.
The proposition supplies a foundational argument for religious narrative by claiming that value reasoning necessarily depends on prior meaning structures rather than bare facts.
Harris's effort to ground values in objective facts while treating stories as useful communications rather than necessary interpretive foundations.
Peterson shares Harris's wish to ground values in truth but argues that access to facts is already mediated by an interpretive framework whose nature requires explanation.
Objective reality and truth rest on fundamental intuitions deeper than religion, and modern inquiry need not represent those intuitions through myth or story.
This offers the secular alternative to Peterson's narrative framework, grounding shared knowledge and rational inquiry in basic intuitions without granting religion representational priority.
Peterson's claim that facts require an a priori interpretive structure best understood partly as a personality or story.
Harris argues that sanity and communication presuppose a distinction between reality and fantasy, while conceding that inquiry ultimately relies on unanalyzed foundational intuitions.
Stories can function as a priori moral intuitions, and Harris's own contrast between maximal misery and flourishing already relies on constructed narrative poles resembling hell and heaven.
The argument aims to show that secular moral realism itself depends on story-shaped moral orientation, thereby narrowing the asserted divide between Harris's framework and religion.
Harris's assertion that foundational intuitions of truth and arithmetic are deeper than religion and are not best captured through stories.
Peterson recasts the moral landscape's worst and best possible lives as fictionalized abstractions and argues that extending them naturally produces the religious categories of hell and heaven.
The worst possible misery for every conscious being is objectively bad and provides an irreducible foundation that makes all other value judgments intelligible.
This is Harris's core account of secular moral realism and his proposed endpoint to regress about value, directly contesting the need for a religious or narrative foundation.
Peterson's argument that Harris merely stakes an a priori moral proposition and has not shown the judgment to be an objectively verifiable fact.
Harris describes universal maximal suffering, argues that denying its badness empties evaluative language of meaning, and treats the judgment as foundational like irreducible intuitions elsewhere.
Moral facts require intermediary intuitions, often embodied in stories, that reveal malevolent agency as an irreducible dimension of hell beyond suffering alone.
The move directly supports religious narrative as a necessary interpretive structure while challenging a suffering-only account of moral evil.
Harris's claim that the worst possible misery grounds intelligible judgments of moral badness.
After accepting the practical endpoint of Harris's regress, Peterson argues that intuitions mediate facts and that stories capture the malevolence producing suffering.
The moral landscape already incorporates intentions, character, psychological consequences, social relations, and every condition capable of affecting conscious well-being.
This reply blocks the claim that secular consequentialism overlooks malevolence, intention, character, or the inner costs of harmful conduct.
Peterson's contention that Harris's account of hell omits malevolent agency and the pleasure taken in causing suffering.
Harris answers Peterson's distinction between suffering and malevolence by expanding the consequential picture to include mental states, intentions, relationships, and society.
Fundamentalists gain rhetorical force from literal textual meaning, while religious moderates make dogma palatable by importing values absent from the originating worldview.
It challenges rehabilitation of inherited religious texts by arguing that humane reinterpretation tacitly rejects rather than faithfully derives from their authority.
The suggestion that fundamentalist adherence has a functional advantage because religious stories operate as evolutionary heuristics.
Following discussion of religious heuristics, Harris explains why literalists can expose the external moral assumptions used to soften unacceptable scriptural commands.
The deepest religious texts place truthful knowledge-updating above dogmatic reliance, symbolized in Christianity by the Word mediating order and chaos.
The move presents religious tradition itself as containing a principled mechanism for revising inherited heuristics rather than demanding static faith.
The conclusion that evolved religious stories cannot be trusted by faith because their usefulness may belong only to past environments.
After agreement that inherited stories may lose relevance, Peterson argues that profound traditions subordinate dogma to the process by which knowledge is updated.
Peterson must specify what God means and what God-like commitment supposedly prevents a real atheist from becoming morally unrestrained.
The challenge demands a clear referent and causal moral role for God-language at the heart of the dispute over religious grounding.
Peterson's repeated claims that he acts as though God exists and that genuine atheism would loosen moral restraints.
Harris presses Peterson to identify the God he acts as though exists and explain what indispensable moral function that God-shaped commitment performs.
God can be understood as the trans-temporal reality expressed through truth, evolved value structures, conscience, sacrifice, judgment, and selection toward competent moral hierarchy.
This is the chunk's principal constructive definition of God-language and connects religious symbolism to truth, evolution, value, conscience, and social order.
Harris's request for a precise account of the God Peterson acts as though exists and its role in moral behavior.
Peterson answers by describing God across long timeframes as the representation of enduring reality, highest value, conscience, sacrifice, and truth-guided selection.
Redefining God as an abstract relation to truth or the unseen changes the traditional noun without establishing the personal supernatural being most believers mean.
The analogy attacks the semantic legitimacy of religious pragmatism by arguing that abstraction wins agreement only through equivocation about ordinary belief.
Peterson's abstract, evolutionary, and trans-temporal definition of God and suggestion that many believers share its intuitions.
Harris uses belief in ghosts as an analogy, arguing that substituting a novel abstract definition does not vindicate what ordinary religious believers traditionally assert.
Penitent reflection that sincerely asks how to repair wrongdoing functions as an answered prayer because an unwelcome corrective answer can emerge from the process.
The example supplies a concrete pragmatic mechanism for prayer, connecting God-language to conscience, confession, moral insight, and behavioral repair.
The challenge to explain concretely how the non-supernatural God Peterson described could hear or answer a prayer.
Peterson asks listeners to imagine a wrongdoer confessing, seeking repair, and accepting any answer, then identifies the resulting corrective insight as answered prayer.
Incompatible Christian, Hindu, and Buddhist moral narratives show that useful religious heuristics cannot establish any one tradition as the deeper truth.
Religious diversity directly undermines the inference from a tradition's meaning or utility to its truth and motivates a deeper nonsectarian explanatory level.
Peterson's claim that evolved religious stories can preserve useful structures their original authors did not consciously understand.
Harris argues that traditions with irreconcilable accounts of good and evil can each provide meaning, so their utility must arise from something deeper than doctrinal truth.
Cross-disciplinary consilience can constrain infinite interpretation by treating patterns repeated across religion, biology, philosophy, neuroscience, emotion, and play as independently real.
The move offers a method for finding a deeper framework beneath competing traditions while resisting both arbitrary interpretation and nihilistic collapse.
Harris's objection that incompatible religious systems require an explanatory level deeper than either Christianity or Hinduism being true.
Peterson accepts the pluralism problem, warns that equal utility can produce nihilism, and proposes consilience across independent domains as a reality check on interpretation.
Cross-cultural disagreement about evil and other moral concepts undermines claims that religious traditions converge on one universal moral pattern.
The move tests whether religious and cultural plurality supports Peterson's claimed universals or instead reveals incompatible moral assumptions.
Peterson's claim that recurring patterns across disciplines and traditions disclose realities independent of interpretation.

After Peterson grounds interpretation through convergence across multiple domains, Harris argues that traditions can reverse moral judgments while allowing that some deeper human universals may remain.
Local moral differences can coexist with deep universals, just as diverse languages and stories share structures that identify their common form.
This move supplies the principal mechanism by which religious diversity can remain compatible with universal moral and narrative structures.
Harris's contention that divergent cultures and religions can invert moral judgments and frustrate claims of universal agreement.
Peterson distinguishes environment-specific adaptations from deeper common structures, argues that good stories share a canonical pattern, and says even factual judgment rests on prior intuitions.
Moral intuitions form a hierarchy in which the deepest intuitions function universally across contexts, analogously to fundamental scientific truths.
The hierarchy answers the objection that dependence on intuition makes every intuition equally credible, preserving a basis for universal moral truth.
Harris's objection that acknowledging intuitive foundations does not make all claimed intuitions equally respectable.
Following the Joseph Smith counterexample, Peterson distinguishes narrow, impulsive intuitions from profound context-independent ones and treats Harris's own moral poles as an instance of the latter.
Calling a deep moral intuition God may be defensible in isolation, but it misleads because ordinary believers generally use God-language differently.
The claim directly contests whether Peterson's revised God-language clarifies moral truth or shelters conventional supernatural interpretations through ambiguity.
Peterson's identification of the deepest context-independent moral intuitions as the relevant foundation for God-language.

Harris grants that Peterson's abstraction could be called God, then shifts the dispute to linguistic and social consequences because common religious usage carries substantially different commitments.
Ambiguous religious language predictably validates unsupported beliefs because it fails to distinguish Peterson's abstraction from the Bible's supernatural and barbaric claims.
This develops the debate's central practical objection to religious pragmatism: sophisticated reinterpretation can lend credibility to dogmas it does not actually endorse.
Peterson's defense that he never claimed his account of divinity was identical to what conventional believers mean.

Harris argues that disclaiming explicit endorsement is insufficient when rhetoric lets audiences preserve supernatural beliefs, comparing the effect to vague appeals that appear to legitimate pseudoscience.
Religious heuristics are unreliable because they work for obscured reasons, whereas rational inquiry can identify enduring concerns without invoking mythology.
The argument directly supports replacing inherited religious rules with open inquiry capable of retaining valid concerns while adapting to changed circumstances.
The proposed reconciliation that adaptive religious stories may encode behaviorally useful guidance even without literal supernatural truth.
Harris says a fixed story can miss changed conditions because it does not track the variables that make its guidance useful, while secular psychology and sociology can address genuine harms directly.
Even beneficial religious dogma remains vulnerable to new knowledge because its rules are blind to the causal variables that actually produce their benefits.
The move explains why accidental adaptive success cannot justify dogmatic authority once inquiry can isolate the genuine causal mechanisms at work.
Peterson's contention that rational educational interventions often change behavior less effectively than inherited narrative constraints.
Harris argues that dogma is also behaviorally limited and, even when historically adaptive, collapses as an epistemic guide once discoveries reveal which variables actually matter.
Discarding the religious edifice risks losing genuine wisdom, because Enlightenment rationality arose through a long developmental history that secular accounts understate.
The claim defends preservation and careful distillation of tradition by treating modern rationality as historically dependent on inherited cultural development.
Harris's claim that identifying the true causal variables makes the surrounding scriptural and dogmatic edifice dispensable.

Peterson resists wholesale collapse of tradition, emphasizes the difficulty of separating wisdom from error, and argues that rational Enlightenment achievements emerged from antecedent cultural processes.
A worldview continuously corrected through honest engagement with reality is better than one anchored to unchanging ideas created without modern tools or knowledge.
This is the secular side's core epistemic standard and directly states why revisable inquiry should replace fixed ancient religious frameworks.
Peterson's warning that Enlightenment rationalism understates its developmental inheritance and may discard valuable traditional wisdom.
After Peterson stresses the historical roots of Enlightenment thought, Harris proposes continuous reality-based correction as the decisive advantage over anchoring belief to ancient, fixed ideas.
Evolved interpretive structures mediate every encounter with facts and generate moral intuition, so value cannot simply be extracted from presently observed facts alone.
The move states Peterson's foundational challenge to Harris's fact-based moral realism by locating value-laden interpretation prior to conscious factual inference.
Harris's proposal that continuous honest engagement with apprehensible reality provides a superior and revisable worldview.

Peterson accepts the need for broad principles, then argues that billions of years of life interacting with reality produced inherited structures that mediate facts and supply the intuitions both sides use.
